During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

Beginning with the most directly connected candidate, CD79B appears particularly relevant to arthritis, especially autoimmune forms such as rheumatoid arthritis. CD79B is a core component of the B cell receptor signaling apparatus, and the cited functional description emphasizes its phosphorylation-dependent role in transmitting antigen-induced signals, including cooperation with kinases involved in nuclear factor kappa B activation and Bruton tyrosine kinase signaling. These pathways are highly pertinent to arthritis because aberrant B cell activation contributes to autoantibody production, antigen presentation, cytokine release, and the maintenance of synovial inflammation. In rheumatoid arthritis and related inflammatory arthritides, dysregulated B cell receptor signaling is mechanistically linked to the survival and activation of autoreactive B cells, which in turn promote chronic joint inflammation and tissue damage. The involvement of CD79B in pre-B cell receptor and B cell receptor signaling, as well as in signaling outcomes such as apoptosis and growth arrest, further suggests that alterations in this axis could influence immune tolerance and the persistence of pathogenic B cell clones. Therefore, CD79B stands out as a biologically meaningful arthritis-related protein because it lies at the center of B cell signaling networks that are already therapeutically implicated in autoimmune joint disease.[PubMed:12563261](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12563261) [PubMed:14662906](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14662906) [PubMed:2404338](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2404338) [PubMed:7608542](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7608542) [PubMed:7690139](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7690139) [PubMed:9636152](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9636152) [PubMed:7592958](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7592958) [PubMed:9177269](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9177269) [PubMed:7565679](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7565679) 

Extending from B cell signaling to innate lymphocyte crosstalk, NCR3LG1 is also of substantial interest in the context of arthritis because it connects innate immune activation with cytokine-driven inflammation. The described function indicates that NCR3LG1 activates natural killer cells and promotes the production of tumor necrosis factor alpha and interferon gamma, two cytokines with well-established roles in inflammatory arthritis. Tumor necrosis factor is a central pathogenic mediator in rheumatoid arthritis and other inflammatory joint diseases, and interferon gamma can shape synovial immune responses, macrophage activation, and antigen presentation. In addition, the ability of NCR3LG1 and natural cytotoxicity triggering receptor 3 signaling to influence dendritic cell maturation suggests a broader role in coordinating innate and adaptive immunity, potentially enhancing the presentation of arthritogenic antigens and sustaining chronic inflammation in the joint microenvironment. Although the provided entry does not explicitly mention arthritis, this protein remains notable because it is mechanistically linked to natural killer cell activation, dendritic cell crosstalk, and cytokine pathways that are highly relevant to synovitis and immune-mediated joint damage.

In a somewhat different but still potentially related direction, PIGR may have a more indirect but still meaningful connection to arthritis, especially in forms of disease in which mucosal immunity and immunoglobulin A biology are implicated. Its function in the assembly and transport-related handling of polymeric immunoglobulin A and immunoglobulin M suggests relevance to immune exclusion at mucosal surfaces and to the regulation of secretory antibody responses. This is noteworthy because increasing evidence links mucosal immune dysregulation, particularly involving immunoglobulin A responses, with the initiation or amplification of autoimmune arthritis, including rheumatoid arthritis. Immunoglobulin A autoantibodies and mucosal immune activation have been associated with preclinical rheumatoid arthritis and with disease heterogeneity. Thus, although PIGR is not a canonical arthritis gene, its role in polymeric immunoglobulin biology makes it plausibly relevant to mechanisms that connect barrier immunity, antibody maturation, and systemic autoimmunity.

Finally, because no functional annotation was supplied for IGLC2 in the input, its relevance to arthritis cannot be assessed directly from the provided evidence. In general, immunoglobulin constant-region genes can reflect B cell and plasma cell activity, which is often important in autoimmune arthritis; however, without a specific functional description or cited evidence, no robust mechanistic interpretation should be made here.

### Placenta; syncytiotrophoblasts - microvilli[High] (HPA:0381223) 

The pathway labeled “Placenta; syncytiotrophoblasts - microvilli[High]” refers to the abundant formation and maintenance of microvilli on the apical surface of placental syncytiotrophoblasts. Syncytiotrophoblasts form the outer multinucleated epithelial layer of chorionic villi and are directly bathed by maternal blood in the intervillous space. Their microvilli markedly expand the exchange surface for oxygen, nutrients, metabolites, hormones, and signaling molecules, while also contributing to barrier function, mechanosensing, and immunological communication at the maternal fetal interface. In this context, a high microvillus state may be viewed as reflecting structural and functional integrity of the placental exchange membrane. The cited literature further suggests that disruption of this state is associated with pathological stress responses. In acute coronavirus disease 2019, syncytiotrophoblasts show loss of microvilli, vacuolization, apoptosis, and endothelial injury, together with villous stromal swelling and reduced vascular lumen, findings that are consistent with hypoxia, energy deficiency, inflammation, and malperfusion. Similarly, elevated particulate matter exposure is associated with shortened and lost microvilli, endoplasmic reticulum stress, basement membrane thickening, mitochondrial injury, and biochemical evidence of oxidative stress. A broader review of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy further places syncytiotrophoblast and villous dysfunction within a framework of endothelial dysregulation, inflammatory signaling, impaired vascular growth factor balance, and placental hypoxia. Taken together, this pathway may be most appropriately understood as a marker of preserved placental epithelial surface specialization, whereas its reduction may indicate oxidative, inflammatory, and vascular injury.

Against this biological background, the relationship between this pathway and arthritis appears indirect, but it remains biologically plausible through shared mechanisms of chronic inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and immune dysregulation. The pregnancy hypertension review explicitly identifies rheumatoid arthritis as a maternal condition associated with increased risk of hypertensive placental disease, thereby placing arthritis within a clinical context in which abnormal placental villous signaling and syncytiotrophoblast dysfunction may be relevant. In that review, placental disease is linked to endothelial overactivity, inflammatory states, hypoxia, and disturbed vascular signaling involving vascular endothelial growth factor, placental growth factor, soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase, soluble endoglin, transforming growth factor signaling, and reduced corin dependent natriuretic peptide activation. These processes may provide a mechanistic bridge to arthritis because inflammatory arthritis is likewise characterized by systemic endothelial activation, cytokine driven vascular injury, and oxidative stress. The two morphology based studies further support this connection by showing that loss of syncytiotrophoblast microvilli occurs in settings of inflammatory and oxidative injury. Acute coronavirus disease 2019 placentas display microvillus loss together with apoptosis, endothelial dysfunction, placentitis, hypoxia, and malperfusion, while particulate matter exposure causes microvillus shortening and loss accompanied by endoplasmic reticulum stress, mitochondrial damage, and increased oxidative stress markers. Although these studies are not arthritis studies per se, they suggest that the microvillus rich syncytiotrophoblast phenotype is highly sensitive to categories of injury that are also central to arthritis pathobiology. Therefore, in patients with arthritis, especially inflammatory forms, this pathway may be interpreted not as an arthritis specific pathway but rather as a placental structural program that could be secondarily perturbed by the systemic inflammatory and vascular milieu associated with arthritis, potentially contributing to adverse pregnancy related outcomes rather than to joint pathology itself.[PubMed:40505896](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40505896) 

With this conceptual link established, the enrichment results provide a more specific view of how arthritis associated proteins may converge on this placental program. There were 19 arthritis-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway labeled “Placenta; syncytiotrophoblasts - microvilli[High].” This enrichment highlights a protein set linked to preservation of the placental syncytiotrophoblast apical surface, where dense microvillus architecture supports a large exchange interface for oxygen, nutrients, metabolites, hormones, and signaling molecules, while also contributing to barrier integrity, mechanosensing, and immunological communication at the maternal fetal interface. In the biological context summarized for this pathway, a high microvillus state may represent structural and functional integrity, whereas reduction of this state is associated with pathological injury patterns that include microvillus loss, vacuolization, apoptosis, endothelial injury, stromal swelling, reduced vascular lumen, endoplasmic reticulum stress, mitochondrial damage, oxidative stress, inflammation, hypoxia, and malperfusion. Thus, the enrichment of 19 proteins in this pathway suggests that the analyzed arthritis related protein set may converge on processes related to epithelial surface specialization, oxidative and inflammatory stress responses, and vascular dysfunction.

To further contextualize these 19 proteins, the figure below illustrates their protein-protein interaction network, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided here for direct network exploration.

![PPI Network](imgs/61a2d58b-6f6b-4288-9524-22af2c595214.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=4D5563F4CFED12CD)

Building on this network-level view, the functional enrichment analysis identified several significant proteins that may help clarify how this pathway intersects with arthritis related biology. We introduce these proteins in greater detail below.

ACE2 is notable in the context of arthritis because vascular dysfunction, endothelial activation, and thromboinflammatory processes are increasingly recognized as important components of chronic inflammatory joint disease. Its vasodilatory and antithrombotic activities suggest a protective role in limiting microvascular injury and platelet driven inflammation within synovial tissues. In arthritis, particularly rheumatoid arthritis, impaired endothelial homeostasis and reduced nitric oxide bioavailability contribute to synovial hypoxia, leukocyte recruitment, and persistent inflammation. Therefore, ACE2 may be mechanistically relevant through its ability to counterbalance these processes and potentially restrain inflammatory vascular remodeling.

In a related manner, ACTA2 may also be relevant to arthritis because cytoskeletal remodeling underlies several pathogenic processes in the arthritic joint, including fibroblast-like synoviocyte migration, myofibroblast-like contractility, and vascular smooth muscle responses. In inflammatory arthritis, activated stromal cells acquire invasive properties that promote pannus formation and cartilage destruction. Although the provided annotation is general, the role of ACTA2 in motility and contractile architecture makes it a plausible marker of mesenchymal activation, tissue remodeling, and synovial invasion rather than a direct immune mediator.

Along similar lines, BSG stands out less for direct canonical arthritis biology than for its broader implications in cell adhesion and tissue interaction. Adhesion molecules are central to leukocyte trafficking, synovial cell communication, and matrix remodeling in inflamed joints. While the supplied functional description emphasizes neural rather than synovial biology, the adhesive and regulatory properties of BSG suggest potential relevance to inflammatory tissue organization and chronic damage responses. This may be particularly pertinent in arthritis associated pain, neuroimmune crosstalk, or tissue remodeling, although the direct connection appears weaker than for immune or vascular regulators.[PubMed:12089450](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12089450) [PubMed:27922006](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27922006) [PubMed:7533044](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7533044) [PubMed:10625334](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10625334) [PubMed:7516497](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7516497) [PubMed:9262180](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9262180) [PubMed:9469574](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9469574) [PubMed:9482781](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9482781) [PubMed:9482783](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9482783) [PubMed:26335717](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26335717) [PubMed:15953602](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15953602) [PubMed:19158290](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19158290) [PubMed:17640868](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17640868) 

Moving from adhesion related processes to adaptive immunity, CD74 appears highly relevant to arthritis because antigen presentation through major histocompatibility complex class two pathways is a central mechanism in autoimmune joint inflammation, especially rheumatoid arthritis. By controlling peptide loading onto major histocompatibility complex class two molecules, CD74 directly influences the repertoire of antigens presented to cluster of differentiation four positive T cells. This is important for the initiation and perpetuation of autoreactive immune responses against joint associated or post translationally modified self antigens. Thus, CD74 can be linked to fundamental disease mechanisms involving adaptive immunity, T cell activation, and chronic synovial inflammation.

Consistent with the importance of immune cell trafficking, CD99L2 is particularly interesting for arthritis because leukocyte extravasation into the synovium is a defining event in inflammatory joint disease. The ability of CD99L2 to facilitate passage through the endothelial basement membrane places it at a critical checkpoint in immune cell recruitment. In rheumatoid arthritis and related inflammatory arthritides, sustained infiltration by neutrophils, monocytes, and lymphocytes drives synovitis and tissue destruction. A molecule functioning at this late transmigration step could therefore contribute directly to persistent inflammatory cell accumulation within joints and may represent a biologically meaningful mediator of synovial inflammation.

From the perspective of innate immune sensing, COLEC12 may also be relevant to arthritis because innate immune activation and clearance of modified self components are important in chronic synovial inflammation. Its ability to recognize microbes supports a possible role in triggering or amplifying inflammatory responses, while its capacity to internalize oxidized low density lipoprotein links it to oxidative stress and damage associated molecular patterns, both of which are increasingly implicated in joint pathology. In arthritis, macrophages and endothelial cells encounter oxidatively modified lipids and inflammatory debris within the joint microenvironment; thus, COLEC12 may contribute to inflammatory sensing, phagocytic clearance, and vascular inflammatory interactions.

In contrast to these more direct inflammatory mediators, GFRAL is not a classical arthritis effector, but it may still be relevant to systemic features of inflammatory disease. Chronic arthritis is often accompanied by fatigue, anorexia, weight loss, and altered metabolism, all of which can be influenced by inflammatory mediators. The growth differentiation factor fifteen and glial cell derived neurotrophic factor family receptor alpha like axis is specifically linked to stress induced appetite suppression and metabolic adaptation, suggesting possible relevance to cachexia-like or constitutional manifestations in severe inflammatory arthritis. However, compared with proteins involved directly in immune trafficking, antigen presentation, or vascular inflammation, its connection appears more indirect and likely pertains to systemic disease burden rather than local joint pathology.[PubMed:28846097](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846097) [PubMed:28846098](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846098) [PubMed:28846099](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846099) [PubMed:28953886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28953886) [PubMed:31152154](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31152154) [PubMed:31928886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31928886) [PubMed:32723474](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32723474) [PubMed:33593916](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33593916) [PubMed:35202387](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35202387) [PubMed:36630958](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36630958) [PubMed:37380764](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37380764) [PubMed:31875646](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31875646) [PubMed:32661391](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32661391) 

Returning to immune regulation more directly, LAIR1 is one of the strongest arthritis related candidates in this list because it functions as a broad immune checkpoint that dampens both innate and adaptive immune activation. Its inhibitory effects on T cells, B cells, natural killer cells, cytokine production, and dendritic cell differentiation are highly pertinent to autoimmune arthritis, where loss of immune tolerance, excessive cytokine signaling, and pathogenic B cell and T cell responses sustain chronic synovitis. By suppressing interleukin two, interferon gamma, immunoglobulin G, immunoglobulin E, interleukin eight, interleukin ten, and tumor necrosis factor related outputs and limiting nuclear factor kappa B activation, LAIR1 may act as an endogenous brake on inflammatory circuits that otherwise promote joint damage. Reduced LAIR1 signaling or ineffective inhibitory tone could therefore plausibly contribute to persistent synovial inflammation and autoimmunity.

Closely related to this vascular and inflammatory framework, NOS3 also stands out as highly relevant to arthritis because angiogenesis and endothelial activation are central to pannus formation and maintenance of chronic synovitis. The annotation emphasizes vascular endothelial growth factor driven signaling, endothelial migration, permeability, and nitric oxide pathway activation, all of which are hallmarks of inflamed synovial tissue. In rheumatoid arthritis, expanded microvasculature supports leukocyte entry, nutrient delivery to hyperplastic synovium, and perpetuation of inflammatory signaling. Molecules participating in vascular endothelial growth factor dependent endothelial responses therefore have strong mechanistic links to disease progression, especially in relation to synovial neovascularization and vascular permeability.

Extending this discussion to oxidative membrane injury and lipid turnover, PLA2G15 may be relevant to arthritis because lipid remodeling and oxidized phospholipid metabolism are increasingly appreciated as contributors to inflammatory signaling and tissue injury. Its ability to hydrolyze truncated oxidized phospholipids suggests a protective detoxification role during oxidative stress, a condition strongly associated with inflamed arthritic joints. In addition, phospholipid metabolism in macrophages and lysosome related compartments can influence antigen processing, inflammatory mediator generation, and resolution of tissue damage. Therefore, PLA2G15 may be important in controlling lipid derived inflammatory cues and limiting oxidative membrane damage in the synovial environment.[PubMed:10092508](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10092508) [PubMed:11790796](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11790796) [PubMed:20410020](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20410020) [PubMed:23958596](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23958596) [PubMed:25727495](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25727495) [PubMed:29724779](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29724779) [PubMed:30830753](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30830753) [PubMed:36823305](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36823305) 

Finally, TFPI2 is highly pertinent to arthritis because extracellular matrix remodeling is a major determinant of cartilage erosion, synovial invasion, and joint destruction. By inhibiting plasmin mediated proteolysis, TFPI2 could influence activation of matrix degrading cascades and thereby modulate tissue breakdown. Its additional effects on coagulation related proteases are also noteworthy, as coagulation and fibrinolytic pathways intersect with inflammatory signaling in arthritic joints. Consequently, TFPI2 may participate in the balance between destructive matrix turnover and protective restraint of protease activity within the inflamed synovium.

### Skin 2; fibrohistiocytic cells[High] (HPA:0471443) 

The pathway labeled “Skin 2; fibrohistiocytic cells[High]” most plausibly denotes a skin tissue program enriched in fibrohistiocytic stromal cells, a mesenchymal lineage that includes fibroblast-like and histiocyte-like cells involved in extracellular matrix remodeling, inflammatory cue integration, antigen-presenting cell support, and tissue repair. In immunobiological terms, such a pathway is not a single canonical signaling cascade, but rather a cellular state characterized by high abundance or activation of stromal cells that can shape local immunity through cytokine production, matrix turnover, leukocyte recruitment, and cross-talk with dendritic cells and T cells. This concept appears highly relevant to inflammatory arthritis because fibroblast-like stromal cells are central effectors of persistent synovial inflammation, invasive pannus formation, cartilage destruction, and resistance to therapy. Evidence from rheumatoid arthritis indicates that fibroblast-like synovial cells may acquire pathogenic properties, including survival advantages mediated by autophagy and high mobility group box chromosomal protein 1, thereby sustaining inflammation and reducing methotrexate sensitivity. In parallel, skin-directed studies indicate that the skin immune microenvironment contains tightly regulated interactions among innate lymphoid cells, dendritic cells, and adaptive immune populations, suggesting that stromal-rich skin states could contribute to pre-arthritic immune priming, especially in diseases that link skin and joint inflammation such as psoriatic arthritis. Taken together, a fibrohistiocytic cell-high skin pathway may be understood as a barrier-tissue stromal and immune interaction module with potential to influence arthritis initiation, propagation, and therapeutic response.

Building on this biological interpretation, the available literature supports a meaningful, although still cautious, connection between a skin fibrohistiocytic cell-high pathway and arthritis through two complementary mechanisms: first, stromal cell pathogenicity as a direct driver of chronic joint inflammation, and second, skin immune dysregulation as a potential upstream site of arthritis-promoting immune activation. In rheumatoid arthritis, fibroblast-like synovial cells are established disease effectors, and one relevant study demonstrated that these cells resist methotrexate-induced death by activating autophagy through high mobility group box chromosomal protein 1 and Beclin 1, indicating that fibroblast-dominant mesenchymal programs may sustain inflammatory persistence and treatment resistance in arthritis tissues (PubMed:26702616). This concept is consistent with broader rheumatoid arthritis biology showing that disease progression can be delayed by early modulation of T cell co-stimulation with abatacept in individuals at risk, implying that tissue-resident stromal and immune networks may already be active before overt synovitis becomes clinically manifest (PubMed:38364839). The skin dimension is particularly important for psoriatic arthritis and possibly for preclinical rheumatoid arthritis because skin immune set points are shaped by local cellular interactions; notably, a recent study showed that skin type 2 innate lymphoid cells regulate dendritic cell homeostasis and activation, thereby influencing downstream adaptive immunity in a sex-dependent manner, which provides a mechanistic framework whereby a stromal-rich skin niche could facilitate inflammatory immune priming relevant to arthritis susceptibility (PubMed:38574174). Additional studies in psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis further support a skin-to-joint axis by showing that altered memory T helper cell states accompany early and subclinical psoriatic arthritis, even before a fully established arthritic phenotype is present (PubMed:35045868), and that early biological treatment targeting interleukin 17 improves both skin and axial articular manifestations, consistent with shared pathogenic circuits across barrier tissue and musculoskeletal compartments. Collectively, these findings suggest that a “Skin 2; fibrohistiocytic cells[High]” pathway may mark a pro-inflammatory stromal microenvironment in the skin that either mirrors or contributes to the fibroblast-centered, immune-amplifying processes that characterize arthritis, especially in rheumatoid arthritis through fibroblast pathogenicity and in psoriatic arthritis through coordinated skin and joint immune activation.[PubMed:26702616](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26702616) [PubMed:38364839](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38364839) [PubMed:38574174](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38574174) [PubMed:35045868](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35045868) 

With this conceptual background in place, the enrichment results provide a quantitative layer of support for the potential relevance of this pathway to arthritis biology. There were 25 arthritis-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway labeled “Skin 2; fibrohistiocytic cells[High],” a stromal and immune-interaction program that appears highly relevant to arthritis because fibrohistiocytic mesenchymal cells contribute to extracellular matrix remodeling, inflammatory signal integration, leukocyte recruitment, tissue repair, and persistence of pathogenic fibroblast-like states within inflamed joint and barrier tissues. In the context of arthritis, the enrichment of 25 proteins in this pathway supports a quantitatively substantial involvement of stromal-cell-centered biology, consistent with the concept that fibroblast-like pathogenic programs may amplify chronic inflammation, promote invasive tissue behavior, and shape cross-talk with dendritic cells and T cells, thereby influencing disease initiation, propagation, and treatment response. Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 25 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is also provided for direct network exploration.

![PPI Network](imgs/5448f650-7fd7-4667-afa3-ee0f5fa39db6.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=4FC372F3B58265F4)

To further clarify how this enriched set may relate to arthritis, the function enrichment analysis highlighted several proteins with plausible immunological, stromal, and vascular relevance. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

CD14 is one of the most arthritis-relevant proteins in this list because it sits at the interface between innate immune sensing and inflammatory cytokine production, two central features of inflammatory joint disease. Its ability to initiate lipopolysaccharide- and lipopeptide-driven signaling through toll-like receptor pathways directly connects it to nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells activation and downstream release of proinflammatory mediators, which are major drivers of synovitis, macrophage activation, and tissue destruction in rheumatoid arthritis and related arthritides. The relevance of CD14 is particularly strong in the context of arthritis because synovial macrophages and monocytes are abundant in inflamed joints, and exaggerated innate immune activation is known to amplify tumor necrosis factor, interleukin 1, and interleukin 6 signaling networks. Moreover, CD14-dependent recognition of microbial products is mechanistically pertinent to forms of arthritis in which infection or dysregulated host-microbe interactions may contribute to disease initiation or exacerbation. Thus, among the listed proteins, CD14 stands out as a plausible upstream regulator of joint inflammation and a marker of pathogenic innate immune activation.[PubMed:16148141](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16148141) [PubMed:15895089](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15895089) [PubMed:8612135](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8612135) [PubMed:19362712](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19362712) 

In a closely related manner, the next protein further emphasizes the importance of macrophage-centered biology within chronically inflamed tissues. CD163 is highly relevant to arthritis because macrophage activation is a defining feature of chronically inflamed synovium. The note that soluble CD163 may be anti-inflammatory and can monitor macrophage activation is especially important in arthritis research, where macrophage-derived pathways strongly correlate with disease activity, synovial inflammation, and therapeutic response. In rheumatoid arthritis, activated synovial macrophages contribute to pannus formation, cytokine production, and joint damage; therefore, a macrophage-associated marker such as CD163 has both mechanistic and biomarker significance. Its anti-inflammatory implication also raises the possibility that CD163 reflects compensatory pathways attempting to restrain tissue injury. For these reasons, CD163 stands out as a clinically meaningful molecule for understanding inflammatory burden and potentially stratifying arthritis severity.

Beyond macrophage activation alone, complement-associated mechanisms may provide an additional layer through which innate immunity contributes to joint pathology. Although the provided annotation emphasizes microbial interaction with Epstein-Barr virus, C1QA remains noteworthy in arthritis because complement activation is deeply implicated in synovial inflammation and immune complex-mediated tissue injury. Complement components contribute to leukocyte recruitment, vascular permeability, and amplification of inflammatory cascades within arthritic joints. C1q-related biology is also relevant to clearance of immune complexes and apoptotic debris, processes that are often dysregulated in autoimmune arthritis. The specific mention of Epstein-Barr virus is additionally interesting because viral triggers have long been investigated as possible contributors to autoimmunity, including rheumatoid arthritis. Therefore, C1QA may be relevant not only through complement-mediated inflammation but also through potential links between infection, aberrant immune activation, and chronic joint disease.

Shifting from soluble inflammatory systems to cell trafficking, adhesion-related proteins may help explain how inflammatory cells accumulate and persist within diseased joints. ICAM3 is relevant to arthritis because leukocyte adhesion, retention, and clearance are central determinants of synovial inflammation. Through its interaction with beta-2 integrins, ICAM3 may influence immune-cell communication and trafficking within inflamed tissues. Particularly important is its role in the phagocytosis of apoptotic neutrophils by macrophages, since defective clearance of dying inflammatory cells can prolong synovitis and promote secondary necrosis, thereby intensifying tissue damage. Neutrophils are abundant in inflammatory joint effusions, especially in active rheumatoid arthritis and crystal-associated arthritis, making molecules involved in their resolution biologically meaningful. Thus, ICAM3 may contribute both to leukocyte recruitment and to the resolution phase of inflammation, two processes that are often imbalanced in arthritis.[PubMed:1448173](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1448173) [PubMed:23775590](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23775590) 

Consistent with this trafficking theme, transendothelial migration represents another necessary step for sustaining inflammatory infiltrates in synovial tissue. CD99L2 is of particular interest in arthritis because leukocyte extravasation into synovial tissue is a prerequisite for persistent joint inflammation. Its role in enabling immune cells to cross the endothelial basement membrane places it directly within the cellular trafficking machinery that supports synovitis. In inflammatory arthritis, the accumulation of monocytes, macrophages, and other leukocytes in the joint is a major pathogenic event that sustains cytokine production and tissue destruction. Proteins that regulate this late step of transmigration are therefore mechanistically significant, as they may determine the intensity and persistence of inflammatory infiltrates. CD99L2 consequently stands out as a plausible contributor to immune-cell entry into arthritic joints and a potential modulator of inflammatory burden.

Alongside immune-cell influx, vascular remodeling is another major feature of chronically inflamed synovium, making angiogenesis-related proteins especially informative. COL18A1 is highly relevant to arthritis because pathological angiogenesis is a hallmark of chronically inflamed synovium. Expansion of the synovial microvasculature supplies nutrients, facilitates leukocyte entry, and supports pannus formation, thereby promoting disease persistence and joint destruction. The anti-angiogenic properties of COL18A1, including inhibition of vascular endothelial growth factor A-kinase insert domain receptor signaling and endothelial migration, suggest that it may function as an endogenous brake on these processes. This is particularly important in rheumatoid arthritis, where vascular endothelial growth factor-driven neovascularization is strongly linked to active synovitis. Therefore, COL18A1 stands out as a protein with a potentially protective role, and its biology may be informative for understanding how angiogenic balance influences arthritis progression.[PubMed:9459295](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9459295) [PubMed:11257123](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11257123) 

In contrast, other enriched proteins may point toward pathways that promote rather than restrain stromal expansion and vascular growth. FGFBP1 is notable in the context of arthritis because it integrates growth factor signaling, cell proliferation, and angiogenesis, all of which are central to synovial hyperplasia and pannus development. Its ability to support fibroblast growth factor and integrin-mediated signaling, together with its potent mitogenic and pro-angiogenic effects, suggests that it could enhance fibroblast-like synoviocyte expansion and vascular remodeling in inflamed joints. These processes are especially relevant to rheumatoid arthritis, where excessive synovial proliferation and neovascularization sustain chronic inflammation and facilitate invasive tissue behavior. In contrast to anti-angiogenic regulators such as COL18A1, FGFBP1 may represent a pathway that promotes the pathogenic stromal response in arthritis. Its functional profile therefore makes it one of the more compelling candidates for involvement in joint remodeling and persistent inflammation.[PubMed:8663044](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8663044) [PubMed:28302677](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28302677) [PubMed:1721615](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1721615) [PubMed:3732516](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3732516) [PubMed:3964259](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3964259) [PubMed:23469107](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23469107) [PubMed:29501879](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29501879) 

Related to this vascular context, stress-response proteins may also shape how stromal and endothelial compartments adapt to persistent inflammation. HSPB6 may have a meaningful, although more indirect, connection to arthritis through its roles in cellular stress responses, vascular regulation, and angiogenesis. Arthritis is characterized by chronic inflammatory stress within the joint microenvironment, and chaperone proteins can influence how stromal and vascular cells respond to inflammatory injury. The reported association with kinase insert domain receptor-related angiogenesis is of particular interest because vascular remodeling contributes to synovial expansion and leukocyte recruitment. In addition, stress-protective proteins may affect the survival of resident joint cells exposed to cytokine-rich conditions. While HSPB6 is not as directly implicated in immune activation as CD14 or CD163, its functions suggest potential relevance to the vascular and stress-adaptation components of arthritis pathobiology.

From vascular adaptation, the discussion naturally extends to cytoskeletal organization, which underlies the invasive behavior of pathogenic stromal cells. ACTA2 is relevant to arthritis because cytoskeletal remodeling and cell motility are essential for the behavior of myofibroblast-like and smooth muscle-like cells in inflamed synovium and vasculature. In chronic arthritis, activated fibroblast-like synoviocytes acquire invasive properties that depend on actin dynamics, enabling migration, matrix remodeling, and cartilage invasion. ACTA2 is also often associated with contractile stromal phenotypes, which may contribute to tissue remodeling and fibrosis-like changes in long-standing disease. Although ACTA2 is a general structural protein rather than a specific inflammatory mediator, its role in motility makes it biologically relevant to the aggressive stromal phenotype that characterizes destructive arthritis.

A similar logic applies to additional regulators of actin dynamics and adhesion, which may further influence synovial lining expansion and tissue invasion. ENAH may be relevant to arthritis because actin remodeling, adhesion, and proliferative control are central to the pathogenic behavior of synovial fibroblasts. In inflammatory arthritis, fibroblast-like synoviocytes display enhanced spreading, migration, and invasive interactions with cartilage and extracellular matrix. A protein such as ENAH, which regulates cytoskeletal organization and adhesion, could therefore influence the structural and migratory properties of these cells. Its reported role in proliferation control is also notable, given that synovial lining hyperplasia is a key pathological feature of rheumatoid arthritis. Although the evidence provided does not directly mention joint disease, ENAH stands out as a plausible modulator of stromal-cell behavior relevant to arthritis progression.

In addition to structural regulators, receptor-mediated signaling pathways may modulate how inflammatory and stromal cells respond to the joint microenvironment. KIT is potentially relevant to arthritis because receptor tyrosine kinase signaling affects mast cells, progenitor cells, and stromal responses, all of which can contribute to joint inflammation. The specific annotation emphasizes negative regulation of KIT through ubiquitination, which is important because dysregulated receptor signaling can amplify inflammatory or tissue-remodeling responses. In arthritis, mast cells and stromal cells have been implicated in cytokine production, vascular changes, and local immune activation; thus, mechanisms controlling KIT abundance may influence disease intensity. While this entry is less direct than those for innate immune receptors or adhesion molecules, KIT remains of interest as part of the broader signaling networks that modulate inflammatory cell function in the joint.

Finally, cell-cycle regulation provides another perspective on how persistent synovial expansion may develop over time in inflammatory disease. MAD1L1 has a more indirect but still potentially meaningful connection to arthritis through its role in cell-cycle control. Synovial hyperplasia in inflammatory arthritis reflects, in part, aberrant proliferation and persistence of stromal and immune cells. Proteins governing mitotic fidelity may therefore influence the expansion, survival, or stress responses of these cell populations. Although MAD1L1 is not a canonical inflammatory mediator, pathways controlling cell division can shape the aggressive phenotype of synovial tissue, especially in rheumatoid arthritis where fibroblast-like synoviocytes exhibit tumor-like proliferative features. Thus, MAD1L1 may be of interest as a marker of proliferative activity rather than a primary driver of inflammation.[PubMed:15024386](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15024386) [PubMed:29162720](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29162720) [PubMed:10700282](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10700282) [PubMed:11804586](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11804586)

### specific granule (GO:0042581) 

The specific granule is a secretory organelle that is characteristic of mature neutrophils and contains a membranous, tubular internal architecture. It stores a defined set of antimicrobial and inflammatory proteins, including lactoferrin, lysozyme, vitamin B12 binding protein, and elastase, many of which are released into the extracellular space during neutrophil activation. In biologic terms, this pathway represents the formation, storage, mobilization, and exocytosis of neutrophil specific granule contents, together with their downstream effects on host defense and tissue inflammation. Because neutrophils are among the earliest and most abundant leukocytes recruited to inflamed joints, the specific granule pathway is highly relevant to inflammatory arthritis. Its cargo proteins can amplify inflammation, remodel extracellular matrix, influence cytokine networks, and contribute to the formation of neutrophil extracellular traps. Lactoferrin is particularly important as a canonical constituent of neutrophil specific granules and has been used as a highly selective marker of neutrophils in inflammatory settings, including experimental arthritis. Thus, the specific granule pathway is best understood as a core neutrophil effector program that links granulocyte maturation to degranulation, extracellular antimicrobial defense, and collateral tissue injury in chronic joint disease.

Against this biologic background, the cited studies collectively suggest that the specific granule pathway may be linked to arthritis primarily through neutrophil activation, degranulation, and release of granule-derived inflammatory mediators within the joint microenvironment. A key piece of evidence is that lactoferrin, one of the defining proteins of neutrophil specific granules, serves as a highly specific neutrophil marker and can localize inflammatory foci in a mouse arthritis model, indicating that specific granule biology is active at sites of articular inflammation and may be exploited to monitor disease-associated neutrophil accumulation (PubMed:29478905). Additional support comes from rheumatoid arthritis transcriptomic work showing that circulating neutrophils display marked phenotypic plasticity and that expression of neutrophil granule protein genes predicts therapeutic response to tumor necrosis factor inhibition, implying that granule-related neutrophil states are mechanistically tied to disease heterogeneity and inflammatory signaling in rheumatoid arthritis (PubMed:27733572). The relevance of granule pathways is further strengthened by the observation that dipeptidyl peptidase one, a granule-associated protease activator in immune cells, correlates with arthritis severity in collagen-induced arthritis rats, suggesting that granule protease activation tracks with disease progression (PubMed:27771442). Although one cited study focuses on antifungal immunity rather than arthritis, it demonstrates that Bruton's tyrosine kinase is required for neutrophil activation, oxidative burst, and granule release, reinforcing the broader principle that signaling pathways controlling neutrophil degranulation can strongly shape inflammatory tissue responses and may therefore represent plausible regulators of arthritic pathology (PubMed:38696257). The importance of granule-derived products also intersects with neutrophil extracellular trap biology, because extracellular traps are composed in part of granule proteins and have been implicated in gouty arthritis as both inflammatory amplifiers and regulators of crystal containment, highlighting how granule cargo can participate directly in joint inflammation and tissue damage (PubMed:41254711). Finally, several arthritis studies in the list converge on tumor necrosis factor, nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells, toll-like receptor four, and nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain-like receptor pyrin domain containing three inflammasome signaling as central inflammatory axes in rheumatoid arthritis, and these pathways are well known drivers and consequences of neutrophil activation and degranulation, providing a disease context in which specific granule release is likely to contribute to synovitis, cartilage injury, and sustained innate immune activation (PubMed:41866004, PubMed:41389887, PubMed:39608616). Taken together, the available evidence suggests that the specific granule pathway may be more than a marker of neutrophil presence in arthritis and could represent a functional effector system influencing inflammatory burden, protease activity, extracellular trap formation, and treatment responsiveness across inflammatory joint diseases.[PubMed:29478905](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29478905) [PubMed:27733572](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27733572) [PubMed:27771442](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27771442) [PubMed:38696257](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38696257) [PubMed:41254711](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41254711) [PubMed:41866004](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41866004) [PubMed:41389887](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41389887) [PubMed:39608616](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39608616) 

Consistent with this literature-based interpretation, the enrichment analysis also points to a quantitatively substantial neutrophil-centered signal.

There were 18 arthritis-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway describing the neutrophil specific granule secretory organelle, a mature granulocyte compartment that stores antimicrobial and inflammatory mediators such as lactoferrin, lysozyme, vitamin B12 binding protein, and elastase. This enrichment highlights a quantitatively substantial neutrophil-centered functional module, with 18 proteins converging on a biological program that integrates granule formation, intracellular storage, mobilization, exocytosis, extracellular host defense, and inflammation-associated tissue injury. In the context of arthritis, this result is biologically plausible because neutrophils are among the earliest and most abundant inflammatory leukocytes recruited into affected joints, and specific granule cargo proteins can intensify cytokine signaling, promote extracellular matrix remodeling, support neutrophil extracellular trap formation, and amplify persistent synovial inflammation. The presence of lactoferrin as a canonical constituent of this granule class further strengthens the interpretation, since it is widely regarded as a highly selective neutrophil marker in inflammatory settings, including experimental arthritis. Overall, the enrichment of 18 proteins in this pathway supports the view that neutrophil degranulation and specific granule biology represent a central effector axis linking innate immune activation to chronic joint damage in arthritis.

To complement this functional interpretation, the interaction structure of the enriched protein set is shown below.

The protein-protein interaction network visualization of these 18 enriched proteins is provided below, together with the link to the STRING webpage for interactive exploration.

![PPI Network](imgs/4f91e3e1-5091-414d-88c3-5422f1e3c7f0.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=344FB51402E27797)

Building on this network-level overview, the following section introduces several of the significant proteins identified in the enrichment analysis and considers their possible relevance to arthritis in a cautious, mechanism-based manner.

During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.
ITGAV is among the most compelling arthritis-relevant proteins in this list because it sits at the interface of matrix remodeling, synovial cell adhesion, leukocyte trafficking, angiogenesis, and cytokine activation. These processes are central to inflammatory arthritis and joint destruction. In particular, the ability of alpha-V integrin complexes to mediate R-G-D-dependent activation of latent TGF-beta-1 is highly relevant, because TGF-beta signaling contributes to synovial fibroblast activation, tissue remodeling, osteophyte formation in some arthritides, and broader regulation of immune responses. Its broad ligand repertoire, including fibronectin, fibrinogen, osteopontin, laminin, and matrix metalloproteinase-2, further links ITGAV to the inflamed arthritic joint microenvironment, where extracellular matrix turnover and invasive pannus behavior are prominent. The additional roles of ITGAV:ITGB3 in growth factor and IL1B-related signaling strengthen the plausibility that this receptor can amplify inflammatory and reparative pathways in arthritis. Overall, ITGAV stands out as a strong candidate mediator of both structural damage and chronic synovial inflammation.[PubMed:10025398](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10025398) [PubMed:9827803](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9827803) [PubMed:25127859](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25127859) [PubMed:11323698](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11323698) [PubMed:24935931](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24935931) 

From matrix interaction and cytokine activation, the discussion naturally moves to a receptor directly embedded in one of the dominant inflammatory signaling axes in arthritis.

TNFRSF1B is highly relevant to arthritis because tumor necrosis factor signaling is a dominant pathogenic axis in inflammatory joint disease, especially rheumatoid arthritis. The receptor's capacity to regulate nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells and c-Jun N-terminal kinase places it directly within signaling pathways that drive synovial inflammation, cytokine production, leukocyte survival, and resistance to apoptosis in pathogenic stromal and immune cell populations. In arthritis, persistent activation of tumor necrosis factor-responsive pathways contributes to synovial hyperplasia, pain, cartilage degradation, and bone erosion. TNFRSF1B is particularly interesting because it is often associated with cell survival and immunoregulatory effects rather than purely cytotoxic signaling, suggesting that it may shape the chronicity of inflammation by sustaining activated immune cells or synovial fibroblasts. Its linkage to TNF receptor associated factor one and TNF receptor associated factor two and antiapoptotic ubiquitin ligases also supports a mechanistic connection to the abnormal persistence of inflammatory cells within arthritic tissue.

A related aspect of chronic joint pathology is localized proteolysis and tissue invasion, which makes the next candidate especially relevant.

PLAUR is notable in the context of arthritis because plasminogen activation and pericellular proteolysis are integral to extracellular matrix degradation, synovial invasion, and cell migration within inflamed joints. uPAR-driven localization of plasmin formation can facilitate breakdown of matrix barriers and promote activation of protease cascades that contribute to cartilage destruction and pannus invasion. Beyond proteolysis, PLAUR also mediates signal transduction, which may enhance inflammatory cell activation, fibroblast motility, and tissue remodeling. These features are particularly relevant to rheumatoid arthritis, where invasive synovial tissue erodes cartilage and bone. Thus, PLAUR potentially links inflammatory signaling with the degradative microenvironment that characterizes destructive arthritis.[PubMed:15677461](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15677461) 

In parallel with matrix degradation, sustained leukocyte entry into the synovium is another defining feature of inflammatory arthritis.

ADAM8 is of interest for arthritis because leukocyte extravasation into synovial tissue is a defining event in inflammatory joint disease. The accumulation of neutrophils, monocytes, and lymphocytes in the synovium and synovial fluid depends on coordinated adhesion, migration, and tissue entry, and proteins that facilitate this trafficking can materially influence disease severity. If ADAM8 promotes leukocyte extravasation, it may contribute to sustained synovitis by increasing immune cell recruitment into the joint. As a member of the ADAM family, it is also plausibly connected to proteolytic remodeling and cell-cell interaction pathways that are often dysregulated in arthritis. Although the provided annotation is brief, the trafficking-related function alone makes ADAM8 a biologically meaningful candidate in arthritis pathogenesis.

Beyond cell trafficking, innate immune sensing pathways may also help shape the inflammatory character of the joint environment.

CLEC4D stands out because it connects innate immune sensing to downstream inflammatory polarization pathways that are strongly implicated in arthritis. Its activation of spleen associated tyrosine kinase, caspase recruitment domain family member nine, and nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells is particularly relevant, as these signaling modules are central to myeloid-cell-driven inflammation in arthritic synovium. Moreover, its ability to promote T helper type one and T helper type seventeen priming is important because T helper type seventeen-associated cytokine networks, especially those involving interleukin seventeen, are well-established contributors to synovial inflammation, osteoclast activation, and tissue damage. Even though CLEC4D is classically described in antimicrobial immunity, pattern-recognition receptors frequently participate in sterile inflammation through recognition of endogenous danger signals and amplification of myeloid activation. Therefore, CLEC4D may have meaningful relevance to inflammatory arthritis by enhancing antigen uptake, antigen presentation, and pathogenic cytokine programs in the joint.[PubMed:23602766](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23602766) [PubMed:23911656](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23911656) [PubMed:14971047](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14971047) 

Whereas the preceding proteins may promote inflammatory activation, the next molecule is notable because it may instead function as a counter-regulatory signal.

LAIR1 is important in arthritis because it represents an endogenous inhibitory checkpoint capable of restraining excessive immune activation. Arthritis pathogenesis often reflects an imbalance between activating and inhibitory immune signals, and LAIR1 has the potential to dampen multiple arms of the inflammatory response, including T-cell cytokine production, B-cell antibody output, and myeloid differentiation. Its suppression of interleukin two, interferon gamma, tumor necrosis factor, interleukin eight, and interleukin ten-related responses, together with inhibition of nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells signaling in myeloid cells, suggests that reduced LAIR1 activity could favor persistent synovitis, whereas intact or enhanced LAIR1 signaling might be protective. The induction of TGF-beta may be context-dependent in arthritis, potentially contributing either to immune regulation or to tissue remodeling or fibrosis, but the dominant theme is that LAIR1 functions as a brake on inflammation. For this reason, it is a particularly interesting molecule when considering mechanisms of immune tolerance failure in autoimmune arthritis.

This balance between inflammatory activation and inhibitory restraint is closely connected to the structural consequences of disease, particularly bone erosion.

OSCAR is one of the clearest arthritis-relevant proteins in the list because osteoclast differentiation is a central mechanism underlying bone erosion in rheumatoid arthritis and other erosive arthropathies. Proteins that promote osteoclastogenesis directly influence the balance between bone formation and bone resorption, and in inflammatory settings this balance shifts toward pathologic bone loss. Given its specific role in osteoclast differentiation, OSCAR likely contributes to the structural damage phase of arthritis rather than merely inflammation alone. This makes it especially important in diseases where radiographic progression and erosions are major clinical concerns. Even though no citation is provided in the input, the functional annotation itself strongly supports a mechanistic connection to arthritis-associated bone destruction.

In addition to osteoclast-related pathways, antibody-driven activation of myeloid cells may provide another route through which inflammation is amplified.

FCAR may be relevant to arthritis because Fc receptor-mediated immune activation is a key mechanism through which antibodies amplify inflammation. Although immunoglobulin A is less emphasized than immunoglobulin G in many arthritis models, immunoglobulin A-containing immune complexes can activate myeloid cells and promote cytokine release, potentially contributing to synovitis. This is especially pertinent in forms of arthritis where mucosal immunity and aberrant antibody responses are implicated. Because FCAR mediates cytokine production downstream of immunoglobulin binding, it could participate in the inflammatory amplification loop within joints or at extra-articular sites that influence disease initiation. Its importance is therefore moderate but biologically credible, especially in antibody-associated inflammatory arthritis.

The inflammatory landscape of arthritis is also influenced by systemic metabolic signals, which provides context for the next candidate.

RETN is potentially relevant to arthritis because it links systemic metabolic inflammation with innate immune cell recruitment. The chemotactic effect on myeloid cells is particularly important, as monocytes and macrophages are major drivers of synovial inflammation and cytokine production in arthritic joints. Resistin has also been broadly associated with inflammatory states, and its dual role in metabolism and immune activation fits well with the recognized intersection between metabolic dysfunction and chronic inflammatory disease. In arthritis, RETN could therefore contribute to both local leukocyte accumulation and the systemic inflammatory milieu that worsens disease activity. Its role may be especially pertinent in patients with obesity or metabolic comorbidity, where inflammatory adipokines can modify arthritis severity.[PubMed:15064728](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15064728) 

From this systemic perspective, it is also useful to consider proteins that may reflect the broader acute-phase response associated with chronic synovitis.

ORM1 is relevant to arthritis primarily as an acute-phase and immunomodulatory protein. Because inflammatory arthritis is characterized by systemic acute-phase responses, proteins such as ORM1 may reflect or influence disease activity. Its ability to modulate immune responses during the acute-phase reaction suggests that it could participate in the broader host response to chronic synovitis, even if it is not a direct driver of joint destruction. Thus, ORM1 is best viewed as a marker and possible modifier of inflammatory tone rather than a primary pathogenic effector. It may still be useful in interpreting arthritis-associated systemic inflammation.

Finally, returning to innate immune amplification, another lectin family receptor may be relevant through macrophage-centered inflammatory signaling.

Although the provided annotation focuses on dengue virus recognition, the most arthritis-relevant aspect of CLEC5A is its capacity to trigger macrophage inflammatory signaling and cytokine release through TYROBP-dependent pathways. Macrophage activation is a major determinant of synovial inflammation, and receptors that amplify cytokine production can have important pathogenic consequences even outside infectious contexts. Therefore, CLEC5A is of interest as a potential innate immune amplifier in arthritis, particularly if endogenous ligands or inflammatory microenvironments engage similar signaling outputs. Its relevance is more indirect than that of ITGAV, TNFRSF1B, or OSCAR, but it remains mechanistically plausible given the central role of macrophage-derived cytokines in joint disease.[PubMed:18496526](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18496526) [PubMed:21566123](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21566123)
